children: Creditors to Altice International sued on Tuesday, alleging the telecommunication company and its billionaire owner Patrick Drahi orchestrated a multiyear scheme to move billions of dollars out of their grasp.

The complaint by lenders including Arini Capital, Invesco, and Diameter Capital said Altice had fraudulently transferred billions of dollars in value to other Altice entities to "indirectly line the pockets of Drahi." The transactions have left creditors less likely to be repaid, holding debt that has plummeted in value, according to the complaint filed in New York state court.

Drahi's Altice entities and their creditors have been locked in a legal standoff that also covers Altice's U.S. business, Optimum Communications, which was sued two weeks ago by its own creditors on similar allegations of fraudulent asset transfers. Optimum last year accused its creditors of violating antitrust laws by fixing its debt prices and blocking its financing transactions, which they have disputed.
A representative for Altice International declined to comment Tuesday.

Tuesday's complaint follows a notice of default delivered by Altice International creditors in July alleging the company had breached its credit agreement through a series of intercompany loans and asset transfers.

The creditor group, which holds a significant portion of Altice International and its affiliates' roughly $9 billion in secured debt, is asking the New York court to declare an event of default, award damages and unwind the challenged transactions.

The company's past transfers include shifting around $5.4 billion of value in the form of intercompany loans from Altice International and its subsidiaries to its parent company Altice Luxembourg starting in 2021. The holding company has no ability to generate cash to repay creditors and isn't required to repay the loans, which have been extended several times with no compensation or justification, according to the complaint.
Similar asset transfers involving the telecom empire's U.K. and France businesses allegedly weakened the creditors' ability to recover money they were owed, the complaint said.

Altice International lent about $680 million to help another Drahi-controlled entity buy shares in British Telecom, but never got the money back, even after those shares were sold for over $4 billion, according to the complaint. Instead, the loan obligation was allegedly transferred to the parent. Altice International also transferred its Caribbean and Portuguese telecommunications business out of the group of companies backing the creditors' debt, effectively moving those assets out of their reach, the complaint said.

Before that transaction, allegedly referred to internally as "Project Déjà Vu," according to the complaint, Altice Dominicana and Altice Portugal had accounted for nearly 80% of Altice International and its subsidiaries' adjusted Ebitda, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.
